shape.name: Shape I - Reciprocal Teaching (Role-Rotated Comprehension)
shape.description: Reading lesson where students rotate four comprehension roles (Predictor, Clarifier, Questioner, Summariser) while reading a text in sections. The teacher scaffolds, then releases control so students own the comprehension monitoring.
shape.pedagogical_justification: Reciprocal teaching is one of the most robustly supported reading approaches. Meta-analyses consistently show effect sizes of d = 0.32-0.88 on comprehension (Palincsar & Brown, 1984). The four roles make comprehension strategies visible and teachable, transforming passive reading into active strategy use. Unlike Shape E, which tests comprehension after reading, reciprocal teaching builds comprehension during reading.
shape.main_aim_format: By the end of the lesson, learners will have practiced and applied [Predictor/Clarifier/Questioner/Summariser] strategies to comprehend a text about [topic].

example_lesson_plan.header:
Objective:
By the end of the lesson, learners will have practiced and applied the strategies of Predicting, Clarifying, Questioning and Summarising to comprehend an article about the global reading decline and why it matters.
Teacher:
Ed Rush
Date:
[DD-MM-YY]
Duration:
46 minutes
CEFR Level:
B1/B2
Lesson Shape:
I (Reciprocal Teaching)
Materials:
Reading pack 'The Reading Crisis', reciprocal teaching worksheet, slideshow, audio model
Assessment:
Role performances, open-class feedback
Skills:
Reading

stages.stage_aim: To activate schema and set the context
procedure: Display the splash PISA graph on PP. The graph shows Thailand's reading scores falling since 2000.
In pairs, Ss tell each other what the graph shows and why reading well might matter.
Whole-class feedback. Elicit: reading at 15 predicts your future success.
Straw poll: How many of you read a book in Thai or English in the last 12 months? Count hands.
Tell Ss they will read the reading pack about the reading decline.

stages.stage_aim: To introduce the four roles and model one round
procedure: Show Task 1: how one round works. Predict, then read, then Clarify, Question, Summarise.
Name the four jobs: Predictor, Clarifier, Questioner, Summariser. One job per person.
Play the audio model. Point to each role on the worksheet Task 4 as the students speak.
Ss read the model chunk (Task 3) silently: What Is Going Wrong.

stages.stage_aim: To read the first chunk with a specific comprehension role
procedure: Assign the four roles around each group of four. Each person takes one job.
Read the reading pack Chunk 1 silently: Reading at 15 predicts your future.
Each student performs their role. The Predictor speaks before reading; Clarifier, Questioner, Summariser after.
Take notes as you read. The teacher will not talk or give answers.

stages.stage_aim: To apply comprehension strategies to two new chunks with different roles
procedure: Rotate roles one position for Chunk 2: Reading pays at school and at work.
Read silently, then each student performs their new role. Take notes.
Rotate roles again for Chunk 3: Reading can be learned, not born.
Teacher stays silent. Groups manage their own discussion.

stages.stage_aim: To apply comprehension strategies to the final chunk
procedure: Rotate roles one final position for Chunk 4: Thailand's fall is the sharpest.
Read silently, then each student performs their final role.
Groups agree on one-sentence summary of the whole reading pack.

stages.stage_aim: To consolidate understanding and address misconceptions
procedure: Open-class feedback. Ask: What surprised you in the readings? What did your group learn?
Review the four strategies: name them and say what each one helps you do.
If time allows, run the final discussion: say your opinion, give a reason, use an example from the text.

metadata.topic: The Reading Crisis: Why Fluency Matters
materials: The Reading Crisis: Why Fluency Matters More Than Ever, adapted from OECD, Thai Enquirer, Edutopia, and PIAAC research
Reading pack (4 chunks): Reading at 15, Reading pays, Reading can be learned, Thailand's fall
Audio model: Reciprocal teaching predictions and discussion
metadata.main_aim: By the end of the lesson, learners will have practiced and applied the strategies of Predicting, Clarifying, Questioning and Summarising to comprehend the reading pack about the global reading decline and why it matters.
metadata.subsidiary_aim: To discuss opinions about reading using the Opinion-Reason-Evidence framework.
answer_key: 1. What is the main idea of the whole reading pack? The main idea is that reading fluency matters more than ever, and that Thailand's reading scores have fallen sharply.

2. What are the four chunks about? The chunks are about reading at 15 predicting your future, reading paying at school and at work, reading being learned rather than born, and Thailand's fall being the sharpest.

3. Chunk 1: What does the OECD 2023 report say? It says the ability to read fluently at fifteen is one of the strongest signs of future success. The pay gap between strong and weak readers reached 25 percent by the late twenties.

4. Chunk 2: Why does reading help at school and work? A study of university students in Vietnam found English reading proficiency was the single strongest predictor of academic performance. Reading fluency also raises income even for people who do not go to university.

5. Chunk 3: Can reading be learned? Yes. Reading fluency is not fixed at birth. It develops through practice, instruction and exposure. Top performers like Finland, Singapore and Canada read often and were taught well.

6. Chunk 4: What happened to Thailand's score? The PISA reading score fell from 441 in 2012 to 409 in 2015, 393 in 2018 and 379 in 2022, the lowest ever recorded. Thailand now ranks below Vietnam (462) and Malaysia (388).
7. Do you think your reading level now will decide what you do later? Model answer: I think reading well now will help me because the text says reading at 15 predicts future success.

8. Is reading useful in your future job? Model answer: Yes, because almost every job needs you to understand written instructions, and the text says workers who could read complex instructions earned more.
